ILLUSTRATIVE ANSWER
A cooler city starts at street level.

Begin with the places where people spend time: the walk to a bus stop, a school courtyard, a small square. A useful cooling strategy brings shade, water and living ground into these everyday spaces.

Start with shade, then connect it

Think in routes as well as destinations. A leafy park is more useful when people can reach it along shaded streets. Prioritize the gaps between homes, schools, shops and public transport before adding isolated green spaces. 1

Make room for living ground

Trees need room below the pavement as well as above it. Combine planting with permeable surfaces and rainwater capture, then give maintenance a place in the plan from the beginning. The design should work through both dry and wet seasons. 2

Measure the experience, not just the map

A practical pilot compares a few places through the day. Record shade, surface conditions and how people use each space. Pair measurements with conversations about who can rest, wait and move comfortably. 3

The useful question is not “How many trees?” but “Where can someone find relief?”
